fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. Hezekiah, king of Judah, hears the report and tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and enters the house of the LORD (Isaiah 37:1). I think he lets how bad it feels show, and then he walks it straight to God's house.

Here's what the text really says: when Hezekiah, king of Judah, hears the report, he tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth (Isaiah 37:1). So the answer is True, he does tear them. Then he enters the house of the LORD. Torn clothes are a loud way to say "this is serious," friend.

Right on the money, baker. Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and enters the house of the LORD (Isaiah 37:1). I bet that news weighs on him, and the text shows him heading straight to God's house.

That's a spot from this story, but it's not where Hezekiah goes. Earlier, the Rabshakeh, the Assyrian king's messenger, stopped at the aqueduct of the upper pool (Isaiah 36:2). That's where the threats were coming from. Hezekiah goes into the house of the LORD instead (Isaiah 37:1).

Elisha was a prophet, the one called to succeed Elijah (1 Kings 19:16). He just isn't the one in this passage. Hezekiah's officials and the leading priests go to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz (Isaiah 37:2). Not the prophet here, but right idea, friend.

Careful, friend, it's the other way around. Through Isaiah, the LORD says, "Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me." (Isaiah 37:6). So the word is "don't be afraid," not "be afraid." I think that's a good thing for a worried king to hear.

That's right, baker. The LORD tells Hezekiah, through Isaiah, "Do not be afraid of the words you have heard…" (Isaiah 37:6). I bet after torn clothes and sackcloth, those are good words to hear. The message goes to Isaiah, and the LORD's answer comes back through him.

You got it, baker. The LORD says the king of Assyria will hear a rumor "…and return to his own land…" (Isaiah 37:7). The LORD says He will put a spirit in him. That's His word about where the king is headed.

I see you reaching for a battle name, baker. Ashdod isn't the one in this passage, though. The Rabshakeh finds the king of Assyria "…fighting against Libnah." (Isaiah 37:8). Two towns in one verse and I'm already reaching for a map.

That's his point, baker. Sennacherib asks, "Will you then be spared?" (Isaiah 37:11). Then he asks, "Did the gods of the nations destroyed by my fathers rescue those nations…?" (Isaiah 37:12). I think he wants Hezekiah to believe Judah is next.

Sennacherib never says that, baker. He asks, "Will you then be spared?" (Isaiah 37:11). Then he asks whether the gods of the destroyed nations rescued those nations (Isaiah 37:12). I think his point is that Judah's God won't save them, not that God is angry.

He does read it, baker, but earlier. The text says he "…received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD." (Isaiah 37:14). That verse doesn't mention any priests.

You got it, baker. Hezekiah says the Assyrians cast those gods into the fire "…for they were not gods, but only wood and stone…" (Isaiah 37:19). Just a few lines earlier he prays, "You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth." (Isaiah 37:16). He sets those things next to the LORD.
